title: Why half your "winning" A/B tests are false positives, and how to test with theories instead
summary: Jason Cohen explains how stopping A/B tests when they look conclusive (p-hacking) and running many tests at 80-90% confidence produces a flood of false positives, which is why stacked "wins" never add up. His fix: rerun tests, don't stop early, chase large effects, and design each test to validate a theory of the customer.

principles.text: A 'successful' A/B test at 90% confidence is wrong about one time in ten, so a string of tests will produce false wins by chance.
principles.quote: All experiments sometimes give false-positives. An experiment that gives the correct result 95% of the time, still gives the wrong answer 5% of the time.

principles.text: Never stop a test just because it looks conclusive; early random fluctuations often mimic significance and then revert.
principles.quote: when N is small, random fluctuations will often cause a result that looks like "90% confidence of a positive result," whereas if you continue the experiment, the data shifts back into the territory of "negative result."

principles.text: Roughly half of declared A/B wins are false, which is why individual improvements rarely compound into the expected total lift.
principles.quote: Why didn't all those improvements add up? Because they were false-positives.

principles.text: Check wins over the long run: even Shopify finds about a third of short-term significant results vanish within a year.
principles.quote: Of the tests which show statistically-significant improvement in the short-term, 35% of the time the effect disappears over the long run.

principles.text: Protect yourself by rerunning the test, not stopping early, and seeking large effects, which means testing drastic changes over incremental ones.
principles.quote: Large effects are unlikely to be caused by randomness; small fluctuations are far more likely to be false-positives.

principles.text: Make every test validate a theory of the customer; throwing variants at the wall teaches you nothing whatever the result.
principles.quote: Not only is this thoughtless and lazy, it also means **you haven't learned anything, regardless of the result of the test.**
